guide.title: Pacific Heights, San Francisco: the Haas-Lilienthal House, two twelve-acre parks and a ridge of numbered houses
guide.intro: Pacific Heights is a ridge of houses above the north side of San Francisco, and nearly all of them are private, with no opening hours to state. The Haas-Lilienthal House at 2007 Franklin Street, built in 1886, is open for docent-led tours: San Francisco Landmark No. 69, designated on 4 January 1975. Two parks sit on the ridge, Lafayette at 12.48 acres and Alta Plaza at 12.94 acres, both open from 5am to midnight. Houses carrying Article 10 landmark numbers stand on California, Sacramento, Jackson, Pacific, Pierce, Scott and Franklin Streets, and a district of 25 Italianate houses runs along Webster Street. Fillmore Street carries the shops; a counterbalance was installed there in 1895 to work a 24.54 percent grade. The Clay Theatre at 2261 Fillmore Street has been shut since January 2020, with a reopening announced in June 2025.

sections.heading: Houses with numbers
sections.body:
The reason to walk this ridge is the houses, and the reason to trust a particular house is its number. San Francisco keeps a register of individually designated buildings under Article 10 of the Planning Code, and Pacific Heights holds a long run of them, mostly on the east-west streets that climb the hill.

Several carry an entry on both registers. The Haas-Lilienthal House, 2007 Franklin Street, is San Francisco Landmark No. 69, designated on 4 January 1975, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 73000438, on 2 July 1973, and it is open for tours. The Whittier Mansion at 2090 Jackson Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 75, designated on 8 November 1975, and was listed on the National Register, reference number 76000524, on 26 April 1976; on 29 April 1941 its title was transferred to the German Reich, which paid $44,000 in cash for it and used it as its consulate. The Atherton House at 1990 California Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 70, designated in 1975 and listed on the National Register, reference number 79000527, on 31 January 1979, was renumbered from 1950 California Street in 1900 and cut into thirteen apartments in 1923. The Tobin House at 1969 California Street faces it: San Francisco Landmark No. 260, designated in 2008, listed on the National Register, reference number 09000806, on 5 October 2009.

The Spreckels Mansion, 2080 Washington Street, is San Francisco Landmark No. 197, designated on 9 June 1990: three storeys in the French Baroque chateau manner by George Adrian Applegarth and Kenneth A. MacDonald Jr., faced across Washington Street by Lafayette Park, and screened by a very tall hedge planted by the novelist Danielle Steel. The Bourn Mansion, 2550 Webster Street, is San Francisco Landmark No. 38, designated in 1971: red clinker brick in an English townhouse manner, built in 1896 by Willis Polk for William Bowers Bourn II and Agnes Moody Bourn.

Beyond those, a numbered house is often all a visitor gets, and that is worth knowing before you set out. Chambers Mansion and the Richard E. Queen House stand on the same block of Sacramento Street; the Isaac Wormser House, the Lilienthal-Orville Pratt House and the William Vale House on California Street; the Talbot-Dutton, Leale and Ellinwood houses along Pacific; the Gibbs Residence and its caretaker's cottage on Jackson Street; the Edward Coleman House on Franklin Street; the Madame C J Walker House on Pine Street; the Ortman-Shumate House on Scott Street; the Casebolt House on Pierce Street. Every one of them is a private residence, and no source states opening hours for any of them, so none are given here. The C. A. Belden House at 2004-2010 Gough Street, the Dallam-Merritt House at 2355 Washington Street and the Real Estate Associates houses on Clay Street carry a National Register reference number and no city number.

sections.heading: The parks, Fillmore Street and Broadway
sections.body:
Two parks of almost exactly the same size sit a few blocks apart, and both are open all year from 5am to midnight. Lafayette Park, 2101 Washington Street, is 12.48 acres and is bounded by Washington, Sacramento, Gough and Laguna Streets, with two tennis courts, a children's playground, an off-leash dog area, restroom facilities and a picnic area; it gives views toward the Marina district, Alcatraz Island, San Francisco Bay, Buena Vista Park and Twin Peaks. Alta Plaza Park, 2501 Jackson Street, is 12.94 acres, established in 1888, bordered by Jackson to the north, Clay to the south, Steiner to the east and Scott to the west, with the plaza cutting off the east-west continuation of Washington Street and the north-south continuation of Pierce Street. Three hard-surface tennis courts, a small playground at the centre, grass across the northern half and terraced lawns on the southern. The steps at Alta Plaza appear in the 1972 film What's Up, Doc?. They were used without permission and were badly damaged during the chase sequence, and the damage can still be seen. A third, much smaller green is the Presidio Library Mini Park at 3150 Sacramento Street, 0.679 acres.

Fillmore Street is where the shops are, in the blocks between Bush Street and Broadway. Streetcar service on Fillmore began in July 1895, and the following month the Fillmore Counterbalance was installed to work the 24.54 percent grade between Green Street and Broadway. The area was platted as part of the Western Addition in the 1860s and acquired the name The Fillmore in the 1880s; decorative arches lined the intersections between 1907 and 1943 and were then removed for scrap for the war effort. The Clay Theatre at 2261 Fillmore Street opened around 1913 and closed in January 2020; it is San Francisco Landmark No. 302, designated on 6 May 2022.

Broadway between Divisadero and Lyon is the other walk. San Francisco Heritage publishes a self-guided Broadway walking tour of approximately 15 blocks, 0.8 miles, which it describes as moderate with a few hills. Two of the institutions on it hold whole city blocks and are working schools rather than visitor sites: Convent and Stuart Hall, the Schools of the Sacred Heart, at 2222 Broadway, and the Hamlin School at 2120 Broadway, a private day school for girls from kindergarten to eighth grade. Sarah Dix Hamlin bought the Van Ness Seminary at 1849 Jackson Street in April 1896, the school took her name in 1898, it moved to 2230 Pacific Avenue in 1907, and she died on 25 August 1923. One caution about the name on the Broadway campus: the James C. Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street is a different house on a different hill.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a bus route, a rail line or a station for this ridge, so none is given here. Steer by street addresses instead, and expect to climb between the parallel streets.

The Haas-Lilienthal House at 2007 Franklin Street, San Francisco CA 94109, (415) 441-3000, is shown on docent-led tours. The churches with published visiting arrangements are St. Dominic's at 2390 Bush Street, Congregation Sherith Israel at 2266 California Street, San Francisco CA 94115, (415) 346-1720, and the Swedenborgian Church, whose sanctuary and garden are at 2107 Lyon Street at Washington Street and whose office and mail address is 3200 Washington Street at Lyon Street, (415) 346-6466. Calvary Presbyterian Church is at 2501-2515 Fillmore Street and St. Brigid's Church at 2151 Van Ness Avenue.

The parks are at 2101 Washington Street, 2501 Jackson Street and 3150 Sacramento Street. For food and a bed: b. patisserie at 2821 California Street, San Francisco CA 94115, (415) 440-1700; SPQR at 1911 Fillmore Street, San Francisco CA 94115; Pizzeria Delfina at 2406 California Street, San Francisco CA 94115, 415.440.1189; and Hotel Drisco at 2901 Pacific Avenue, San Francisco CA 94115, (415) 346-2880.

The houses named above are read from the pavement, at 2080 Washington Street, 2090 Jackson Street, 2550 Webster Street, 1990 and 1969 California Street, 2220-2222 and 2212 Sacramento Street, 2395 Sacramento Street, 1782 Pacific Street, 2475 and 2799 Pacific Avenue, 2622-2624 Jackson Street, 1701 Franklin Street, 1834 and 1818-1820 and 2226 California Street, 2066 Pine Street, 1901 Scott Street, 2727 Pierce Street, 2004-2010 Gough Street, 2355 Washington Street and 2503, 2524, 2530 and 2536 Clay Street. The Webster Street district runs three blocks. The Lyon Street stairway climbs between Broadway and Green Street.

faq.question: Can you go inside any of these houses?
faq.answer: Yes, at the Haas-Lilienthal House, on published dates. San Francisco Heritage runs docent-led tours of the Haas-Lilienthal House at 2007 Franklin Street in 2026 on select Wednesdays at 12.30pm and 2pm and Saturdays at noon, 1pm and 2pm. General admission is $10, children twelve and under are free, and San Francisco Heritage members are free; allow at least one hour. The house is wheelchair accessible at ground level through the tour entrance, and an elevator is available for moving between floors. The other great houses on the ridge are private residences or working institutions, and no source states opening hours for them, so none are given here.

faq.question: What are Lafayette Park and Alta Plaza Park like, and when do they open?
faq.answer: Both are open all year from 5am to midnight and both are close to twelve and a half acres. Lafayette Park at 2101 Washington Street is 12.48 acres, or 543,742 square feet, and holds two tennis courts, a children's playground, an off-leash dog area, restroom facilities and a picnic area; it looks toward the Marina district, Alcatraz Island, San Francisco Bay, Buena Vista Park and Twin Peaks. Alta Plaza Park at 2501 Jackson Street is 12.94 acres, or 563,451 square feet, established in 1888, with three hard-surface tennis courts, a playground at the centre, grass on the northern half and terraced lawns on the southern half. Alta Plaza has been recorded by the Historic American Landscapes Survey as HALS No. CA-16.

faq.question: Which churches and synagogues can be visited?
faq.answer: Three publish visiting arrangements. The Swedenborgian Church, whose sanctuary and garden are at 2107 Lyon Street at Washington Street, runs in-depth educational tours every Sunday at 1pm, lasting about an hour, with no reservations required except for large groups; its office and visiting hours are Monday to Friday 10am to 6pm and Sunday noon to 2pm, closed on major holidays except Sundays, and Sunday worship is 11am to noon. St. Dominic's Catholic Church at 2390 Bush Street carries docent tours, a twilight tour hosted by its own docents, a shrine of St. Jude, a columbarium and a mass-times page. Congregation Sherith Israel at 2266 California Street runs historic sanctuary tours. Calvary Presbyterian Church at 2501-2515 Fillmore Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 103, designated in 1978, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 78000755, on 3 May 1978.

faq.question: Is the Clay Theatre showing films?
faq.answer: No. The cinema at 2261 Fillmore Street closed in January 2020 and the building is not open; no source states opening hours. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 302, designated on 6 May 2022. In February 2024 the theatre and the adjacent building were bought by investment trusts linked to Neil Mehta, and in June 2025 the Upper Fillmore Revitalization Project announced plans to reopen the Clay as a 200-seat repertory cinema after renovations to upgrade its facilities and improve fire safety and accessibility.

faq.question: What is the Webster Street Historic District?
faq.answer: A group of 25 Italianate houses built between 1878 and 1880, sharing a vertical emphasis, angled bay windows and a dominant cornice line, running three blocks and taking in 25 parcels. It is San Francisco Landmark District No. 2, designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code by Ordinance 166-81 on 8 April 1981. The houses are private and are read from the pavement.

faq.question: Where can you eat, and where can you stay?
faq.answer: Four operators publish their own addresses. b. patisserie is at 2821 California Street at Divisadero, San Francisco CA 94115, (415) 440-1700, open Wednesday to Friday 8 to 4 and Saturday and Sunday 8 to 5, closed Mondays and Tuesdays; it also runs a sister restaurant at 2794 California Street. SPQR at 1911 Fillmore Street serves a la carte or a $102 four-course menu seven days a week from 5 to 9pm, with a $69 five-course pasta tasting menu on Wednesdays and Thursdays; reservations are through Resy for parties of up to six, and corkage is $40 per 750ml bottle with a two-bottle maximum. Pizzeria Delfina at 2406 California Street offers a menu, pickup and reservations, and states no hours. Hotel Drisco is at 2901 Pacific Avenue, (415) 346-2880, with a dining room and event space.

places.name: Haas-Lilienthal House
places.summary: A Queen Anne house of 1886 on Franklin Street, run by San Francisco Heritage and shown on docent-led tours. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 69, designated on 4 January 1975, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 73000438, on 2 July 1973. It was named a National Treasure by the National Trust for Historic Preservation in 2012. Tours in 2026 run on select Wednesdays at 12.30pm and 2pm and Saturdays at noon, 1pm and 2pm; general admission is $10, children twelve and under free, San Francisco Heritage members free, and the operator advises allowing at least one hour. The house is wheelchair accessible at ground level through the tour entrance, and an elevator is available for moving between floors. Telephone (415) 441-3000.
places.history: The house was built in 1886 for the merchant William Haas and Bertha Greenebaum Haas; the architect was Peter R. Schmidt and the contractors McCann & Biddell. A 1928 addition of living quarters over a garage is attributed to the architect Gardner Dailey. The house withstood the 1906 earthquake with only slight damage. The Haas family watched the fire from the roof and left to camp in Lafayette Park; three days after the earthquake the fire was stopped at Van Ness Avenue. Alice Haas-Lilienthal died in 1972 after living in the house for close to eighty years, and the house was given to the Foundation for San Francisco's Architectural Heritage, now San Francisco Heritage, in 1973.

places.name: Lafayette Park
places.summary: A hilltop park of 12.48 acres, or 543,742 square feet, bounded by Washington, Sacramento, Gough and Laguna Streets. San Francisco Recreation and Parks gives it as open all year from 5am to midnight. It holds two tennis courts, a children's playground, an off-leash dog area, restroom facilities and a picnic area, and gives views toward the Marina district, Alcatraz Island, San Francisco Bay, Buena Vista Park and Twin Peaks.
places.history: The Spreckels Mansion faces the park across Washington Street. No source states a date for the park's creation, so none is given here.

places.name: Alta Plaza Park
places.summary: A terraced park of 12.94 acres, or 563,451 square feet, taking up four blocks: Jackson to the north, Clay to the south, Steiner to the east and Scott to the west, with the plaza cutting off the east-west continuation of Washington Street and the north-south continuation of Pierce Street. Three hard-surface tennis courts, a small playground at the centre, a large grass park on the northern half and terraced lawns on the southern half. Open all year from 5am to midnight.
places.history: The park was established in 1888 and has been recorded by the Historic American Landscapes Survey as HALS No. CA-16. The steps at Alta Plaza appear in the 1972 film What's Up, Doc?. They were used without permission and were badly damaged during the chase sequence, and the damage can still be seen.

places.name: Presidio Library Mini Park
places.summary: A mini park of 0.679 acres on Sacramento Street, recorded by San Francisco Recreation and Parks. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the park.

places.name: Spreckels Mansion
places.summary: A three-storey house in the French Baroque chateau manner, completed around 1912 to 1913 for Adolph B. Spreckels to designs by George Adrian Applegarth (1876-1972) and Kenneth A. MacDonald Jr. of MacDonald & Applegarth. It faces Lafayette Park across Washington Street, behind a very tall hedge planted by the novelist Danielle Steel. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 197, designated on 9 June 1990. The house is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The house is reported to have 55 rooms and a Louis XVI ballroom. Eight Victorian homes were moved to Jackson and Washington Streets to clear the combined lots. Alma de Bretteville Spreckels went to Europe to stock the house, met Auguste Rodin on the same trip and brought thirteen of his bronzes back for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition; the Rodin bronzes she brought back later inspired the creation of the California Palace of the Legion of Honor. The exterior served as the nightclub in the 1957 film Pal Joey. The house was divided into apartments after 1968 and later restored to a single residence.

places.name: Whittier Mansion
places.summary: A house built between 1894 and 1896 for William Franklin Whittier (1832-1917), a paint and white-lead manufacturer. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 75, designated on 8 November 1975, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 76000524, on 26 April 1976. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: On 29 April 1941 the mansion's title was transferred to the German Reich, which paid $44,000 in cash for it and used it as its consulate. The California Historical Society occupied the building later. The San Francisco Chronicle reported the transfer in April 1941, and it is also recorded in the Historic American Buildings Survey.

places.name: Bourn Mansion
places.summary: A house of red clinker brick in an English townhouse manner, built in 1896 for William Bowers Bourn II and Agnes Moody Bourn to a design by Willis Polk. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 38, designated in 1971. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Atherton House
places.summary: A house of 1881 to 1882 built for Dominga de Goni Atherton (1823-1890), widow of Faxon Atherton and mother-in-law of the novelist Gertrude Atherton. Queen Anne blended with Stick and Eastlake work: horizontal lines, a clipped gable and a short tower. The architect is thought to be John Marquis. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 70, designated in 1975, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 79000527, on 31 January 1979. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The house was renumbered from 1950 to 1990 California Street in 1900. Later owners included Edgar Mills, brother of Darius Ogden Mills of the Bank of California, and from 1908 George Chauncey Boardman. The architect Charles J. Rousseau bought it in 1923 and subdivided it into thirteen apartments; his widow Carrie lived there with fifty cats until her death in 1974.

places.name: Tobin House
places.summary: A house on California Street, opposite the Atherton House. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 260, designated in 2008, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 09000806, on 5 October 2009. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its two register entries.

places.name: Talbot-Dutton House
places.summary: A house on Pacific Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 57, designated in 1973. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Leale House
places.summary: A house on Pacific Avenue. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 45, designated in 1972. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Ellinwood House
places.summary: A house at the Pacific Avenue corner. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 207, designated in 1994. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Gibbs Residence and Caretaker's Cottage
places.summary: A house on Jackson Street with its caretaker's cottage, designated together. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 203, designated in 1993. Both are private and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the buildings beyond their register entry.

places.name: Chambers Mansion
places.summary: A house on Sacramento Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 119, designated in 1980. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Richard E. Queen House
places.summary: A house on the same block of Sacramento Street as the Chambers Mansion. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 198, designated in 1990. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Health Sciences Library
places.summary: A building on Sacramento Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 115, designated in 1980. No source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the building beyond its register entry.

places.name: Edward Coleman House
places.summary: A house on Franklin Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 54, designated in 1973. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Isaac Wormser House / John C. Coleman House
places.summary: A house on California Street carrying two family names in the register. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 53, designated in 1973. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Lilienthal-Orville Pratt House
places.summary: A house on California Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 55, designated in 1973. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: William Vale House
places.summary: A house on California Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 168, designated in 1984. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Madame C J Walker House
places.summary: A house on Pine Street, entered in the city register as the Madame C J Walker House, Home for Girls. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 211, designated in 1999. It is private and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Ortman-Shumate House
places.summary: A house at the Scott Street corner. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 98, designated in 1977. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Casebolt House
places.summary: An Italianate house of about 1865, built for Henry Casebolt to designs by the architects Hoagland and Newsom. Four storeys and roughly 5,875 square feet. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 51, designated on 5 March 1973. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a further history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: C. A. Belden House
places.summary: A house on Gough Street carrying a federal entry and no city number. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 83001229, on 11 August 1983. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: Dallam-Merritt House
places.summary: A house on Washington Street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 84001185, on 19 April 1984. It is a private residence and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the house beyond its register entry.

places.name: The Real Estate Associates Houses
places.summary: Four speculative houses on one block of Clay Street, at 2503, 2524, 2530 and 2536, entered on the federal register as one group. They were listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 85000705, on 4 April 1985. All four are private residences and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Real Estate Associates, known as TREA, was the developer that built 2115-2125 Bush Street and 1942-1948 Sutter Street. It put up more than a thousand houses in the Mission, the Western Addition and this ridge during the 1870s, selling to the working-class market on easy credit.

places.name: Webster Street Historic District
places.summary: A run of Webster Street covering three blocks and 25 parcels. It is San Francisco Landmark District No. 2, designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code by Ordinance 166-81 on 8 April 1981.
places.history: The district takes in 25 Italianate houses built between 1878 and 1880, sharing a vertical emphasis, angled bay windows and a dominant cornice line. The houses are in private hands and are read from the pavement.

places.name: Congregation Sherith Israel
places.summary: A domed synagogue at the north-east corner of California and Webster Streets, by the architect Albert Pissis, who trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts. The building stands 140 feet above California Street, the dome is 60 feet in outside diameter, and the interior holds 20,000 square feet, 3,500 organ pipes and seating for 1,385. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 10000114, on 31 March 2010. The congregation's own site carries historic sanctuary tours, its Czech Torah, its organ and a seismic retrofit. Telephone (415) 346-1720.
places.history: The site was bought on 8 September 1902, ground was broken on 8 October 1903, the cornerstone was laid on 22 February 1904 and the sanctuary was consecrated on 24 September 1905, at a cost of $250,000. The synagogue was a principal site of the San Francisco graft prosecution trials held between 1905 and 1908.

places.name: Calvary Presbyterian Church
places.summary: A church with a columned portico at the corner of Fillmore and Jackson Streets. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 103, designated in 1978, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 78000755, on 3 May 1978.
places.history: No source states a history of the church beyond its two register entries.

places.name: St. Brigid's Church
places.address: 2151 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco, CA 94109
places.summary: A stone church on Van Ness Avenue that no longer functions as a parish. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 252, designated in 2006. No source states visiting hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the building beyond its register entry.

places.name: St. Dominic's Catholic Church
places.summary: A large Gothic Revival parish church at Bush and Steiner Streets. The parish site carries docent tours, a schedule of upcoming tours, a twilight tour hosted by the St. Dominic's docents, a shrine of St. Jude, a columbarium, a mass-times page and a Sermon in Stone page describing the building. It carries no entry on either the city or the federal register.
places.history: No source other than the parish itself states when it was founded, so no founding date is given here.

places.name: Swedenborgian Church
places.summary: A church with a sanctuary and garden at 2107 Lyon Street at Washington Street; the office and mail address is 3200 Washington Street at Lyon Street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 04001154, on 18 August 2004, and is a National Historic Landmark. In-depth educational tours run every Sunday at 1pm and take about an hour, with no reservations required except for large groups; visitors may also drop in during office hours. Office and visiting hours are Monday to Friday 10am to 6pm and Sunday noon to 2pm, closed on major holidays except Sundays, and Sunday worship is 11am to noon. Telephone (415) 346-6466 for the main office and (415) 346-6468 for events.
places.history: No source states the building's construction date, so none is given here.

places.name: Clay Theatre
places.summary: A single-screen cinema on Fillmore Street, closed since January 2020. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 302, designated on 6 May 2022. The building is not open, and no source states opening hours.
places.history: It opened around 1913 to 1914 as The Regent, a nickelodeon that often showed Mary Pickford films; it became The Avalon in 1931 and The Clay International in 1935 under Herbert Rosener, showing foreign film. The exterior was heavily modified in the 1950s, when the ticket booth was moved and the archway entrance changed, and the house latterly held 325 seats. The Clay joined the Landmark Theatres chain in 1991 and closed in January 2020. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 302, designated on 6 May 2022. In February 2024 the theatre and the adjacent building were bought by investment trusts linked to Neil Mehta. In June 2025 the Upper Fillmore Revitalization Project announced plans to reopen the Clay as a 200-seat repertory cinema after renovations to upgrade its facilities and improve fire safety and accessibility.

places.name: Fillmore Street
places.summary: The shopping street of the ridge, running north-south across it. The blocks between Bush Street and Broadway carry the restaurants, bakeries and clothing shops.
places.history: The ground was platted as part of the Western Addition in the 1860s and the area acquired the name The Fillmore in the 1880s. Streetcar service on Fillmore began in July 1895, and the following month the Fillmore Counterbalance was installed to work the 24.54 percent grade between Green Street and Broadway; the Street Railway Journal recorded it in June 1896. Decorative arches lined the intersections between 1907 and 1943, when they were taken down and scrapped for the war effort.

places.name: Broadway between Divisadero and Lyon
places.summary: The run of Broadway west of Divisadero Street, a corridor of very large houses and school campuses. San Francisco Heritage publishes a self-guided Broadway walking tour of approximately 15 blocks, 0.8 miles, which it describes as moderate with a few hills.
places.history: Two working schools hold campuses on this stretch: Convent and Stuart Hall, the Schools of the Sacred Heart, at 2222 Broadway, and the Hamlin School at 2120 Broadway. Sarah Dix Hamlin bought the Van Ness Seminary at 1849 Jackson Street in April 1896; the school took her name in 1898 and moved to 2230 Pacific Avenue in 1907, and she died on 25 August 1923. Neither campus carries an entry on the city or federal register, and the James C. Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street is a different building from the Flood house on Broadway.

places.name: Lyon Street Steps
places.summary: A public stairway climbing Lyon Street between Broadway and Green Street. It carries no entry on either the city or the federal register, and as a public stairway it keeps no hours.
places.history: No source states a history of the stairway.

places.name: b. patisserie
places.summary: A pastry shop at California Street and Divisadero. Its own site gives the hours as Wednesday to Friday 8 to 4 and Saturday and Sunday 8 to 5, closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Telephone (415) 440-1700. The same site names a sister restaurant at 2794 California Street.
places.history: No source states a history of the business.

places.name: SPQR
places.summary: An Italian restaurant on Fillmore Street. Its own site gives a la carte service or a $102 four-course menu seven days a week from 5 to 9pm, and a $69 five-course pasta tasting menu on Wednesdays and Thursdays from 5 to 9pm. Online reservations are through Resy for parties of up to six. Corkage is $40 per 750ml bottle, with a two-bottle maximum.
places.history: No source states a history of the business.

places.name: Pizzeria Delfina, Pacific Heights
places.summary: A pizzeria on California Street, one of four locations the group names on its own site, and the one it calls Pacific Heights. It offers a menu, pickup and reservations, and gives a telephone number of 415.440.1189. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the business.

places.name: Hotel Drisco
places.summary: A hotel on Pacific Avenue with a dining room and event space. Its own contact page gives the address as 2901 Pacific Avenue, San Francisco, California 94115, the telephone as (415) 346-2880 and reservations at reservations@hoteldrisco.com. No source states its rates, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the building or of the business.

entries.name: Haas-Lilienthal House
entries.note: A Queen Anne house of 1886 at 2007 Franklin Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 69, shown on docent-led tours on select Wednesdays and Saturdays for $10.

entries.name: Lafayette Park
entries.note: 12.48 acres bounded by Washington, Sacramento, Gough and Laguna Streets, open 5am to midnight, with tennis courts, a playground and an off-leash dog area.

entries.name: Alta Plaza Park
entries.note: 12.94 acres of terraced lawns established in 1888, open 5am to midnight; its steps appear in the 1972 film What's Up, Doc? and still carry the damage.

entries.name: Spreckels Mansion
entries.note: San Francisco Landmark No. 197, a French Baroque chateau of about 1912 facing Lafayette Park across Washington Street, behind a very tall hedge.

entries.name: Whittier Mansion
entries.note: Built 1894 to 1896 for William Franklin Whittier; on 29 April 1941 its title passed to the German Reich, which paid $44,000 in cash and used it as its consulate.

entries.name: Bourn Mansion
entries.note: Red clinker brick in an English townhouse manner, built in 1896 by Willis Polk; San Francisco Landmark No. 38, designated in 1971.

entries.name: Webster Street Historic District
entries.note: Italianate houses of 1878 to 1880 with angled bay windows; San Francisco Landmark District No. 2, designated by Ordinance 166-81 on 8 April 1981.

entries.name: Swedenborgian Church
entries.note: In-depth tours of about an hour every Sunday at 1pm, no reservation needed for small groups; listed on the National Register, reference number 04001154.

entries.name: Broadway between Divisadero and Lyon
entries.note: San Francisco Heritage publishes a self-guided walking tour of this corridor, approximately 15 blocks and 0.8 miles, which it calls moderate with a few hills.

entries.name: Fillmore Street
entries.note: Streetcars began running in July 1895 and a counterbalance was installed the next month to work the 24.54 percent grade between Green Street and Broadway.

entries.name: Clay Theatre
entries.note: A cinema of about 1913 shut since January 2020; a June 2025 plan would reopen it as a 200-seat repertory house. San Francisco Landmark No. 302.

entries.name: b. patisserie
entries.note: Pastry at California Street and Divisadero, Wednesday to Friday 8 to 4 and Saturday and Sunday 8 to 5, closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

entries.name: SPQR
entries.note: Italian on Fillmore Street: a la carte or a $102 four-course menu daily from 5 to 9pm, with a $69 pasta tasting menu on Wednesdays and Thursdays.

entries.name: Hotel Drisco
entries.note: A hotel at 2901 Pacific Avenue with a dining room and event space; no rates are stated by the operator.

links.note: Down the north slope: the Octagon House and the Sherman House on Gough and Green Streets, the Palace of Fine Arts and the Fort Mason block.
East across Van Ness Avenue: the crooked block of Lombard Street, the Alhambra Theater on Polk Street and three National Register districts.
The next ridge east, holding Grace Cathedral, the Cable Car Museum and the James C. Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street.
